# Gradient Descent and Convergence

Gradient descent is the foundation of all neural network training. Understanding convergence theory — Lipschitz conditions, convergence rates, and loss landscape geometry — is essential for diagnosing training failures and designing better optimizers.

## The Update Rule

θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − η∇f(θₜ). Each step reduces f by ≈ η·‖∇f‖² (to first order). Progress is proportional to gradient magnitude and learning rate.

## Lipschitz Gradient Condition

‖∇f(x) − ∇f(y)‖ ≤ L‖x−y‖ → descent lemma: f(y) ≤ f(x) + ∇fᵀ(y−x) + (L/2)‖y−x‖². With η ≤ 1/L: guaranteed monotone decrease of at least (1/2L)‖∇f‖² per step.

## Convergence Rates

| Setting | Rate | Steps for ε |
|---------|------|-------------|
| Convex, L-smooth | O(1/T) | O(1/ε) |
| Strongly convex, κ = L/μ | Linear O(ρᵀ) | O(κ log(1/ε)) |
| Non-convex | O(1/√T) to stationary | O(1/ε²) |

## Non-Convex Landscapes

Saddle points (∇f=0, indefinite H), flat regions (‖∇f‖ ≈ 0), ravines (ill-conditioned H). Empirically: overparameterised networks have no bad local minima; flat minima generalise better.

## Batch GD vs. SGD vs. Minibatch

Gradient estimate ĝ_B = (1/B)Σ∇Lᵢ is unbiased with variance σ²/B. Larger B → lower variance, more compute, sharper minima. Optimal B is a hardware-vs-generalisation tradeoff.

## Implicit Regularisation of SGD

SGD noise biases toward flat (wide) minima. Full-batch GD finds sharp minima with worse test error (Keskar et al. 2017). This motivates keeping effective batch size moderate even in distributed training.
